Chapter 1: Introduction 

"Once upon a time..."; this is the classical formula with which stories begin. A story has many purposes, such as oral history, communication, and individual or group identity formation (Thompson, 2017). Before Guttenberg invented the printing press, stories were the only viable form of spreading news and gossip. The printing press made the mass production of newspapers possible and feasible (Hoe, 2021). In journalism, narratives or stories are referred to as exemplars (Oschatz et al., 2021). The internet did not change the fundamental human craving for stories; on the contrary, it amplified and increased exemplars' geographical reach and propagation speed through social media (Peters et al., 2022). The impact of a story is greatly influenced by the source's credibility (Seiler & Kucza, 2017). Not only children blindly believe their parents and grandparents when they tell them the story of Little Red Riding Hood. Grown-ups also tend to weigh in their connection to the person from whom they receive information, regardless of the credibility of the initial source of the story (Naskar et al., 2020; Samuel-Azran & Hayat, 2019). The very nature of social media sharing usually implies a well-known and trusted source of the re-shared/re-tweeted story, belonging to the same in-group as the reader (Cheng et al., 2017). Therefore, a viral story has an exponentially higher impact (Flanagin & Metzger, 2017; Naskar et al., 2020). Viral stories use the brain's propensity toward Bayesian statistics and exploit the pars pro toto fallacy of generalization, suggesting a single example represents all instances of the same kind (Lemieux, 2020). The following paragraph will exemplify such pars pro toto cases and how they can impact people's lives as an introduction to this phenomenon. Cambridge Analytica gained notoriety by publicly claiming to have contributed to Donald Trump  ́ s presidency of the United States of America in 2016 through bespoke social media content. Allegedly, the presidential campaign postings were adapted to the specific personality profile of the respective audience (Grassegger & Krogerus, 2016). Dr. Michal 11 Kosinski correlated the patterns of public Facebook 'Like's with traditional NEO PI-R TM 

personality profiles from tens of thousands of research volunteers (Bachrach et al., 2012; Kosinski et al., 2013). A similar project was undertaken by Chen et al. (2016). Chen et al. mined user interactions and assessed them using machine learning and a naïve Bayesian algorithm. Publicly available structural features of online interactions have also been correlated using theoretical inferences for social media personality profiling without connecting to pre-existing self-assessment questionnaires (Golbeck et al., 2011; Jianqiang et al., 2018). The public digital footprint from the social media platform Twitter was successfully used for the same purpose of algorithmic psychometrics (Golbeck et al., 2011; Jianqiang et al., 2018; Quercia et al., 2011). Once the OCEAN (Big Five) personality profile of a reader is known, the content can be adapted to the personality of the reader, thereby increasing the chances of the message to resonate with, be accepted, and be shared online by the reader by psychological targeting (Grassegger & Krogerus, 2016; Matz et al., 2017). Once a story has been brought to the reader's attention by psychological targeting, the personal connection of the sharer with the receiver overrides the impact of the credibility of the initial source and the accuracy of the factual content (Samuel-Azran & Hayat, 2019). The current state-of-the-art analysis method marketing specialists use to trigger virality on purpose is sentiment analysis (Zimbra et al., 2018). Marketing specialists have used sentiment analysis, for example, to trigger the virality needed to promote tourism to Oman (Ramanathan & Meyyappan, 2019), cricket in Bangladesh (Mahtab et al., 2018), energy companies in the UK (Ikoro et al., 2018), or London Heathrow Airport (Martin-Domingo et al., 2019). Drus and Khalid's (2019) literature review gives a good overview of a wide range of further marketing applications. Sentiment analysis determines the valence and arousal level contained within and provoked by a specific text and, thereby, facilitates how well marketing content is performing by 12 determining with the help of emojis and the thumbs-up/down feedback to stories if the reaction to it is positive or negative (Sailunaz & Alhajj, 2019). On the other hand, emotion analysis determines the specific emotion, giving a clue as to why specific content is going viral and, therefore, is much more complex (Xu et al., 2020). Although sentiment and emotion may seem synonymous, especially for non-native English speakers, they describe two completely different approaches from a scientific analysis perspective. Sentiment analysis involves emoji and thumps up/down analysis, all valences on a linear spectrum, whereas emotion analysis strives to determine the exact emotion from the very complex and non-linear pool of human emotions. A standard technical solution to sentiment analysis, facilitated by the spread of emojis and thumbs-up/down, has been found and is now widely used (Sánchez-Núñez et al., 2020). The more complex emotion analysis is still ongoing research in computer science (Sánchez-Núñez et al., 2020). The social sciences could contribute valuable theoretical information toward the emotional analysis of narratives and help decode the exact mechanisms of triggering a viral chain reaction through the seemingly simple means of telling a story. Psychology is the perfect choice among the social sciences to decipher how and by what means emotions mediate the viral stories` impact on people's lives in the age of the internet (Dafonte-Gómez et al., 2020). Psychology has devoted a whole research paradigm to the scientific exploration of how normative and personal life experiences and social conduct are shared through stories (Handler & Theodor, 1987; Schiff, 2017). Narrative Psychology is tasked to explore the mechanisms by which the qualia of story sharing help provide life with meaning (Schiff, 2012). Qualia is the phenomenological Bayesian perception of semiotically generated elements of consciousness (Clark et al., 2019; Harkness, 2020). Building meaning, however, is not the sole purpose a narrative can have. Yale's Nobel Prize laureate Prof. Robert Shiller coined the term Narrative Economics in 2017. He developed an entire 13 theoretical framework explaining how the virality and ease of global information sharing through the internet have repurposed stories to achieve global, political, and economic impact. The influence on financial and legislative decision-making is significant. When it goes viral, the personal relationship to the person by whom a story is shared overshadows the importance of factual content and initial source relevance. The combination of these two factors warrants a deep dive into the psychological components involved in media manipulation. Social and traditional media manipulation, regardless of whether it is purposeful, by design, or incidental, has become an increasingly prevalent occurrence with far-reaching consequences (Ferrara et al., 2020; Krafft & Donovan, 2020; Marwick & Lewis, 2017; Shiller, 2020a; Woolley & Howard, 2018). The anti-vaxxer movement (Benoit & Maldin, 2021), the Fridays for Future climate movement (Brünker et al., 2019), Brexit, the 2016 U.S. elections (Grassegger & Krogerus, 2016), the surge in the value of cryptocurrencies (Nizzoli et al., 2020), or the stock market dives triggered by the news of the spreading Omicron COVID-19 variant (Nelson & Phillips, 2021) are just some recent and preeminent examples of the potential for media manipulation. The World Economic Forum (WEF) has termed this phenomenon digital wildfires and placed it on the top of the list of global risks for developing countries in the hyper-connected world of the 21 st century (WEF, 2013). Mark Zuckerberg's hearing in front of the U.S. Congress in 2018 has brought media manipulation under public scrutiny (González et al., 2019). The critical testimony in front of the U.S. Senate of whistleblower Frances Haugen, a former Facebook employee, brought the social media hegemon’s allegedly disruptive effects back into the public eye (Oxford Analytica, 2021). Narrative manipulation is not exclusively a European and North American problem; it affects South America (van Dijk, 2017), China (Gao, 2017), Africa (Wasserman & Madrid-Morales, 2019), and India (Green & Vasudevan, 2016), making it a global problem. Because media 14 manipulation through narratives is an international problem (Bradshaw & Howard, 2018) with potentially far-reaching economic consequences (Shiller, 2017), psychology could and should contribute to the growing body of research on this topic. Professor Shiller (2017) strongly advised using social media to analyze textual emotion in his original paper. He specifically called for psychology and AI to contribute to the advancement of narrative economics: "Advances in psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence may be relied on to improve our sense of structure in narrative economics." (Shiller, 2017, p. 50). 

Statement of the Problem 

The problem addressed by this dissertation was the potential for media manipulation through the viral spread of narratives with potentially far-reaching economic and political consequences, such as meme stocks, cryptocurrency, or election manipulation (Grassegger & Krogerus, 2016, 2017; Hegazy, 2021; Richterich, 2018; Risso, 2018). As the internet is the medium used to spread narratives, everybody who has access to the internet is potentially affected by them. As of April 2021, 59.5% of the world's population had access to the internet, with Northern and Western Europe having the highest internet penetration rate of well over 90% (Statistica, 2021). Brexit and the 2016 U.S. election manipulation brought this phenomenon into the public spotlight (Grassegger & Krogerus, 2017). A recent example with far-reaching health risk consequences for an entire generation are the popular opinion carriers called the anti-vaxxer digital moms (Weinberg & Dawson, 2020). The anti-vaxxer opinion current was created through the global spread of emotionally triggering narratives (Weinberg & Dawson, 2020). How sentiment is used for such manipulations is known, but the exact role of emotions in the virality of narratives is still not entirely explored due to its complexity (Sánchez-Núñez et al., 2020). The virality of narrative has far-reaching effects on the world's interconnected economies (Shiller, 2020b) and the national democratic processes (Aral & Eckles, 2019; McKay & Tenove, 2021; Woolley & Howard, 2018). Since the COVID-19 15 pandemic, the world's health status (Vériter et al., 2020) remains vulnerable to manipulation by the continued exposure of the entire world population with internet access to emotion-based media manipulation. 

Purpose of the Study 

The purpose of this quantitative cross-sectional design using a structural equation model was to determine if emotions mediate the viral spread of narratives with potentially far-reaching economic and political consequences (Shiller, 2020a). The study only analyzed online content because the problem only affects internet users. While the primary news consumption and spread medium has moved from the media to social media, exemplars still originate in the media outlets because social media has no own journalists (Barthel et al., 2020). The primary producers of exemplars are still the global media outlets, making them the appropriate analysis objects for this study (Thorbjørnsrud & Ytreberg, 2020). The dataset used was the publicly available cloud-based Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone GDELT (Google, 2021), created by Georgetown University. GDELT is updated every 15 minutes from news outlets around the world. For ease of understanding, only English news sources were included in the analysis. Global coverage is available, but since all other languages are translated, the translation adds confounding inaccuracies avoidable by using only English data. The events are pre-classified in root events and subsequent mentions. GDELT contains nominal emotion, topic, and economic measures variables and has been previously used for research purposes by Tilly et al. (2021) and Weigang and Meng (2018). Each and all of these, and only these pre-classified measures were used in the current research, amounting to a total number of 688 variables measured for all events every 15 minutes or a total of 70,080 times during the selected 2-year period between 2020 and 2022. A significant world event sparking viral narratives with substantial economic consequences providing the ideal, high stakes opportunity for psychological targeting and social media 16 manipulation was chosen as a sampling timeframe: the COVID-19 pandemic. The role of emotions as potential mediators of event news spread was analyzed for 2020–2022, and the economic consequences resulting from the spread were determined post-ex factum using a partially latent structural regression model. 

Introduction to the Theoretical Framework 

Narrative economics deals with the economic consequences of spreading narratives (Shiller, 2017). Shiller (2020a) proposed four analysis steps within narrative economics for the process, which he termed narrative modeling: emotion analysis, entity-relation extraction, topic extraction, and subject modeling. Entity-relation and topic extraction have already been technically solved by computer sciences with the help of machine learning, neural networks, and artificial intelligence (Wadden et al., 2019). Subject modeling has been solved with the help of psychology by applying the Big Five OCEAN personality model through algorithmic psychometrics (Stark, 2018). Of the four narrative modeling steps, only one remains unsolved, and psychology can best inform this last piece of the puzzle: the emotion analysis part. The narrative economics theoretical framework has guided the problem statement and the purpose statement by helping to identify a psychological phenomenon with wide-reaching economic consequences worth studying in depth. Emotion dynamics theory provided the guiding theoretical framework to inform the emotion analysis part of the narrative modeling process (Bringmann et al., 2016; Burr et al., 2021; Ernst et al., 2021; Krone et al., 2018; Kuppens & Verduyn. 2017; Naskar et al., 2020; Schneider et al., 2020). Emotion dynamics theory was initially developed by Levenson and Gottman (1983) and further expanded by Kuppens and Verduyn (2017). The principles of emotion dynamics are contingency, inertia, regulation, and interaction (Kuppens & Verduyn, 2017). The principle of contingency states that emotions are typically triggered by external or internal events, often social, raising concerns or 17 influencing the person's well-being. The principle of inertia postulates emotions as resistant to change and always tending to reflect the respective current emotional state. The principle of regulation hypothesizes emotions as tending to fit the current desired state to maintain allostasis. Furthermore, the principle of interaction binds the three aforementioned together by stating the interaction of all the above principles, boosting or canceling each other out dynamically, giving the theory its name. Emotions are not static. They develop in time and have a temporal component. As the principle of interaction states, emotional dynamics can be computer-simulated over time in a three-dimensional space (Becker et al., 2004). The time dimension of emotional dynamics can be represented as an interconnected emotional network and simulated with a Bayesian statistical model (Krone et al., 2018). Emotions can blunt or augment each other in a personal emotional network, as represented by the principle of interaction. Opinions can be changed and influenced over time when emotions are involved, whereby the source of a narrative has the most decisive influence on the decision to share/re-tweet/spread a story and contribute to it going viral (Naskar et al., 2020). While narrative economics provides the general conceptual framework for the purpose of this study and emotion dynamics justifies analyzing emotions as mediators of the spread of viral stories, prospect theory is needed to close the loop and quantify the economic impact of a story's virality. Prospect theory was first proposed by the psychologists Kahneman and Tversky in 1979 as an alternative to up until then valid paradigm of the homo economicus. Prospect theory assumes people do not make entirely rational economic decisions; they are not the "Mr. Spock" the economists of the 20th century presumed them to be. A homo economicus type rationality would dictate buying at the lowest price and selling at the highest price to maximize profit (Pareto & Page, 1906). Prospect theory contrasted this by postulating that from a psychological perspective, people tend to buy when the price rises 18 and sell when the price falls, thereby totally contradicting economic rationality (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Barberis et al. (2016) empirically tested the predictive power of prospect theory regarding economic decision-making related to the stock market. Prospect theory predicts that stocks with a past high performance would be more appealing, triggering buying decisions. The hypothesis was tested with historical data from the U.S. stock market as well as 46 international markets. The authors found evidence to support their hypothesis in the U.S. stock market data from 1931 until 2010 and in most of the 46 international markets from which the trading patterns were analyzed. Barberis et al.´s (2016) work is instrumental in pinpointing psychological theories to help underpin the contribution of the social sciences to the theory of narrative economics. As a decision theory, prospect theory explains how a narrative is interpreted in deciding whether to buy or sell a particular publicly traded stock of a company mentioned in a viral story with a global economic impact. Barberis et al. (2016) suggested that prospect theory is valid for theoretical use in an economic context and in practice for stock return predictions based on trading decisions of small investors. A recent validation of both prospect theory and narrative economics predictions was the GameStop stock hype via Reddit (Chaudhry & Kulkarni, 2021). 

Introduction to Research Methodology and Design 

The study is a quantitative cross-sectional design using secondary data from an existing, publicly available dataset. A partially latent structural regression model was performed to analyze the secondary data. An extensive and representative dataset was used, namely the cloud-based Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone GDELT (Google, 2021), created by Georgetown University, which is publicly available. The entire dataset between the selected years from 2020 until 2022 can be analyzed in Python using the open-source Pandas library with the help of BigQuery (Chen, 2017). Numerous social science and economics analyses have been previously performed on the GDELT dataset using these 19 methods, such as Tilly et al. (2021) and Weigang & Meng (2018). Since it is a secondary analysis of an existing dataset, no data gathering is needed, and no ethical conflicts arise from its use. GDELT's Global Content Analysis Measures (GCAM, 2021) module contains over 2,300 emotions, affect, and valence measurements, and GDELT's Global Knowledge Graph (GKG) contains over 100 supplementary topics and themes, all of which are updated every 15 minutes from news outlets around the world. Assuming English speakers will read the study, exclusively news sources in English were analyzed. GDELT's translated global coverage was excluded to avoid confounding factors. The GKG was used to track events using graph analysis. Global events, pre-classified in root events and subsequent mentions, are coded in the Conflict and Mediation Event Observations (CAMEO) format developed by the Pennsylvania State University (Schrodt, 2012). Their spread is tracked throughout time and worldwide geography every 15 minutes. The complete list of GCAM and GKG variables is attached in Appendix 1. Table 41 in Appendix 1 lists the 396 topics and themes to be analyzed, based on the classification frameworks of Albaugh et al. (2013) and Leetaru and Schrodt (2013). Table 42 in Appendix 1 contains the 288 emotion variables to be analyzed based on the emotional classification frameworks of Dodds et al. (2011), Loughran and McDonald (2011), Martindale (1987; 2019), Miller (1995), Pennebaker et al. (2007), Strapparava and Valitutti (2004). The sheer amount of variables leads to a potential combination of 396 topics possibly influenced in their spread by 288 emotions. The resulting 2.663616654 E+99 possible combinations of potential mediations make mediation analysis unsuitable for this study. Mediation analysis is a subset of path analysis (Hayes, 2017), but emotions tend to overlap and cluster (Peng & Liu, 2018), and the uncertainty of exclusively linear relationships makes path analysis insufficient. However, path analysis is a particular form of structural equation 20 modeling (SEM), which can handle both the sheer amount of potential combinations as well as account for potential emotional clustering and non-linear relationships, making SEM the most suitable methodological design for this study. Especially since the economic effect would be the fourth variable, extending beyond the range of mediation analysis.
