Significance of the Study 

If psychology can scientifically decipher the precise mechanisms underlying mass media manipulation through emotionally charged viral content, it could be theoretically employed to purposefully craft narratives with positive and desirable economic, health, or political consequences through their spread. Psychology could, therefore, establish itself as a social science with the potential to create a measurable economic outcome. Psychology would step out of the shadow and trade its status as an aid to consumer engineering (Armstrong, 2021) to become a principal actor. If the role of emotions were known, it could be possible to create an automatic anti-manipulation defense mechanism by scanning the world news in real-time and detecting the stories with the highest potential for psychological targeting with harmful economic, health, or political consequences. Such a defense mechanism against mass media manipulation could establish psychology as a meaningful contributor to the inner balance of all democracies worldwide that are connected to the internet. Viral narratives can fundamentally change public thinking and motivation (Shiller, 2020c). Especially in the United States of America, words from a prominent leader can shape the mode of thinking of the population with serious economic effects and could mitigate an economic downturn during the COVID-19 pandemic (Shiller, 2020d). Like Franklin D. Roosevelt’s "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself" (White House, 2021), which helped the United States of America out of the great depression, or President Reagan's "Mr. Gorbatschev, tear down that wall" (McMaster, 2021, p. 181), which accelerated the downturn 24 of communist totalitarianism. Instead of leaving the desired effect to chance or determining what the correct narrative could be by trial and error, psychology could provide the missing scientific link and tools to craft and choose powerful, positive narratives. Shiller (2020e) called for more research in quantifying narratives to help establish causality between the narratives and their economic effects, which is what this study is endeavoring to accomplish with the help of psychological emotion dynamics and prospect theory. 

Definitions of Key Terms 

Anti-vaxxers 

A deriding and pejorative term used for people who are against vaccination, re-sparked by Andrew Wakefield (1998; 1999), who linked the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine to autism based on a study of 12 children. Although his research was proven to be false, retracted by The Lancet (The Editors of The Lancet, 2010), and the UK General Medical Council's Fitness to Practise Panel revoked Wakefield´s medical license over it in 2010, the parental concerns over vaccinating their children remained and led to a global increase in the anti-vaccine movement. First, it produced hesitance only against the childhood vaccines, but during the global COVID-19 pandemic, it became a worldwide health risk through the massive refusal of vaccination against the SARS-CoV-2 virus (Dean, 2021). 

Digital Moms 

Yalda Uhls (2016) coined this term describing the paradigm of female parenting in the age of the internet. The internet often provides the only networking means for modern moms who tend to join online support groups, follow parenting blogs, or otherwise seek information and emotional support online during maternity leave. Because these private blogs and online support groups only provide personal opinions stemming from single personal experiences but are often the only source of information readily available, the term digital 25 moms is often used pejoratively to insinuate a gossipy type as opposed to a factually informed mother. 

Exemplars 

Narratives in journalism are called exemplars. They usually contain the story of a person or group of people representative of a broader category, used to exemplify a particular topic, destiny, or to make a point (Oschatz et al., 2021; Skovsgaard & Hopmann, 2020; Zerback & Peter, 2018). 

GDELT 

A publicly available cloud-based Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone (GDELT) created by Georgetown University and updated every 15 minutes with news from media outlets around the world (Google, 2021). 

Narrative Economics 

Nobel laureate Yale Prof. Shiller coined this term and theory, describing how viral narratives can have global economic consequences (2020b). 

Narrative Virality 

In the context of this study, the potential of a narrative to behave like a virus and be spread ideologically from person to person by sharing through mass and social media on the internet (Milner, 2018). 

Pars pro Toto Fallacy 

The human brain tends to wrongly interpret a single example as representative of all instances of the same kind (Lemieux, 2020). 

Python 

An object-oriented, interpreted programming language intended for large-scale projects. It comes with over 300.000 packages supporting data analytics, machine learning, and scientific computing, making it perfectly suitable for Big Data scientific data analysis 26 above and beyond what SPSS can handle. Python was voted the programming language of the year 2021 by the TIOBE Programming Community Index (Tiobe, 2022). 

Qualia 

The subjective experience of how it feels to be or to do something; this state of consciousness can only be experienced but cannot be entirely shared (Harkness, 2020; Clark et al., 2019). Most famously exemplified by the philosopher Thomas Nagel (1974) in his essay about how one can imagine what it would be like to be a bat, but nobody except a bat can ever experience the qualia of what it is really like to be a bat. 

Summary 

The quantitative cross-sectional design using secondary data analysis endeavors to explore a partially latent structural regression model of viral narratives and establish the temporal relationship of emotions as mediators for the spread of a narrative, while the size of the spread and the reach of the story are assumed to determine its potential economic impact. From a theoretical perspective, emotion dynamics and prospect theory operationalized as a structural equation model on the GDELT dataset could be psychology's contribution toward informing and advancing the emotion analysis process within narrative economics. The next chapter will review the literature extensively, identifying the calls for further research to justify this study and the role psychological theory can play in filling the gaps at the intersection of narrative economics and Big Data computer science application. 27 

Chapter 2: Literature Review 

The purpose of this quantitative cross-sectional design using a structural equation model was to determine if emotions mediate the viral spread of narratives with potentially far-reaching economic and political consequences (Shiller, 2017; Shiller, 2020a). This dissertation addressed the problem of potential media manipulation through the viral spread of narratives with potentially far-reaching economic and political consequences, such as meme stocks, cryptocurrency, or election manipulation (Grassegger & Krogerus, 2016; Grassegger & Krogerus, 2017; Hegazy, 2021; Richterich, 2018; Risso, 2018). To that extent, this research applied and operationalized the psychological theory of emotion dynamics (Bringmann et al., 2016; Burr et al., 2021; Ernst et al., 2021; Krone et al., 2018; Kuppens & Verduyn. 2017; Naskar et al., 2020; Schneider et al., 2020), the psycho-economical prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979) and place both within the framework of narrative economics (Shiller, 2017; Shiller, 2020e). Each of these three guiding theories and theoretical frameworks will be discussed individually and in-depth in a subsection of this chapter. As narratives are the principal subject of analysis in this dissertation, a literature review of narratives and exemplars, the term used to describe narratives in the media, as well as their social, political, health-relatives, and economic effects will be presented further on. The other sections include a literature review of emotions, their role as potential mediators and action-triggers, concluding with an overview and a critical evaluation of the existing emotion analysis methods. The literature review was performed using the freely available resources of Northcentral University's (NCU) academic library and Google Scholar. The EBSCOhost Discovery Service (EDS) powering NCU's Roadrunner search has been used to avoid searching each database individually. For seminal articles, no time range restrictions have been used. The search range has been restricted to the last five years for recent publications. Only scholarly/peer-reviewed sources where the full text was available have been used, 28 written in one of the languages the author is fluent in (English, German, or Romanian). This study is multi-disciplinary and, therefore, needs no discipline restriction applied to the searches. Psychology, economics, and other disciplines such as marketing, journalism, political and computer science, and many more have informed this study. A complete list of search terms created with the search history function of the Northcentral University's academic library has been provided in Appendix 5. 

Theoretical Frameworks 

As with any multi-disciplinary study, an integrative view and review of more than one theory are necessary to make sense of the complexity of the interaction of emotions, viral narratives, and economics. Whenever one scientific branch interacts with another, emergence can occur through consilience (Shiller, 2020a). The result is incommensurable and non-reducible to the individual components from which it emerged (Lewes, 1891). A relatively recent and prominent example of consilience was the rescue mission in the Tham Luang Nang Non Cave, in 2018 in Thailand, where it took two very different and highly specialized skillsets to rescue the 13 boys and their coach. The Thai Army´s medical doctor Lt. Col. Pak Loharachun who was a trained Navy SEALs diver was lacking the specialization in anesthesiology and the special skills needed for cave dive rescue operations in confined spaces. Being just a medical doctor and a trained diver was insufficient for the purpose of the mission. The Australian Dr. Richard Harris was both a medical doctor specialized in anesthesiology and an experienced cave rescue diver, which uniquely enabled him to devise a rescue plan through consilience (Ahmed et al., 2021). Such an integrative process of emergence through consilience is currently underway at the intersection between social sciences, economics, and computer science (Buyalskaya et al., 2021; Shiller, 2020a). The result is novel, coherent, evolving, ostensive, and has the property of wholeness at the macro-level (Corning, 2002; Moore et al., 2018; Rosas et al., 2020). The complex, global interaction 29 of narratives, the internet, and the economic effect of the viral spread of memes fulfill all the above-mentioned required properties of weak emergence. In other words, it is not something entirely different to warrant the status of a strong emergence but also non-reducible to its original components, hence being a weak emergence (Bedau, 1997; Rosas et al., 2020). Economics, social, and computer science can each theoretically explain an aspect of and a viewpoint upon reality, but only in combining their respective scientific theories and specific research tools can the emergent result be understood in all its supervenient complexity. Therefore, this research endeavors to integrate economic, psycho-economic, and psychological theories and operationalize their predictive components with a computer science application. Narrative economics, emotion dynamics, and prospect theory were the guiding theoretical frameworks for this study. Each framework will be reviewed separately in the following sections. 

Narrative Economics 

Each society produces scientific paradigms capturing its Zeitgeist, especially during the model crisis stage of the Kuhn-Cycle of scientific revolution (Kuhn, 1963). Smith's (1776), Mill's (1874), and Pareto and Page's (1906) homo economicus started to become inadequate to explain the changing economies of the 21st century, even with the added bounded rationality constraints of behavioral economics (Tversky & Fox, 1995). None of them considered the economic implications of global information spread through the internet because it was not part of their Zeitgeist and went beyond their contemporary technical capabilities. The exponential spread of the internet in all the world's countries caused a model drift of economic theory in the Kuhn-Cycle (Kuhn, 1963). Yale's Nobel laureate Prof. Shiller (2017) proposed with his narrative economics theory a model revolution integrating psychological, technological, and economic factors with both a predictive and explanatory value. The central concept of narrative economics is that an idea, a meme, can spread like and 30 is just as contagious as a virus (Shiller, 2017; Shiller, 2020a). Dawkins (2006) introduced the concept of encapsulating the essence of an idea into a meme with the spreading capabilities of a thought virus. A meme is the basic information unit carrying an idea, a symbol, or a practice, transmissible from mind to mind by any form of known communication (Milner, 2018). The SIR-model, a mathematical theory of disease epidemics, can then be applied to calculate how the thought virus contained in a narrative will spread from mind to mind, from person to person (Kermack & McKendrick, 1927). The SIR-Model postulates that given S as the susceptible population, I the infected, and R the recovered population, then N=S+I+R is assumed to be constant (Kermack & McKendrick, 1927). Thought viruses can also mutate, just like biological, epidemiological viruses (Milner, 2018), through social media by mirroring the effect of the Chinese whispers children’s game (Muppalla, 2018). The reach is determined by the medium through which it is communicated, but the potency of the narrative is the emotional content. Through content mutation, a narrative adapts to different media and cultures, maintaining both its integrity as well as its viral potential (Bomsel, 2020). Narratives provide a coherent and integrative worldview within which actions with economic consequences can occur (Shiller, 2017; Shiller, 2020a). Because the internet made spread via social media facile, the initial source of the narrative is replaced during viral spread by somebody well-known from the in-group, which gives the narrative, not only coherence but also a higher degree of credibility (Cheng et al., 2017). The reach of a narrative and the size of its global spread determine the magnitude of the economic consequences (Shiller, 2017; Shiller, 2020a). Testability and falsifiability are mandatory for a scientific theory to be considered as such (Popper, 1963). Testability requires the theoretical constructs to be operationalized. Narrative economics is operationalized as narrative modeling (Shiller, 2017). Narrative modeling is comprised of four distinct steps: entity-relation extraction, topic extraction, 31 subject modeling, and emotion analysis. These four steps are independent of each other and do not require a particular sequence. 

Entity-Relation Extraction. Entity-relation extraction requires the identification of the actors and the entities a narrative is referring to. The actors could be persons, institutions, countries, political parties, or companies; any entity can constitute a party if it can take or be the recipient of an action. The relation between the entities defines their ties to each other or identifies them as the actor, respectively, or the subject of the action (Shiller, 2017). In 2017 when narrative economics theory was formulated, automated entity-relationship extraction was still somewhat of a technological challenge. 

Meanwhile, computer science has solved this problem, making available fast, inexpensive, and reliable standard solutions (Zhong & Chen, 2020). Not only has it been technically solved, but event data containing entities and their relationship already pre-extracted are publicly available, and there is even a free R-package available (utdeventdata) to analyze the data (Kim et al., 2019). For example, pre-extracted entity relationships are accessible through Harvard's Integrated Crisis Early Warning System (ICEWS) Dataverse, a now close-sourced US-Government project not publicly updated or available for research anymore, primarily intended to detect impending international crises stemming from the relationships between the involved entities (Boschee et al., 2018). Although ICEWS is now close-sourced, the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone (GDELT) created by Georgetown University, is still freely available for public use (Google, 2021). None of them are perfect; the two databases share a variance of only 71%, with GDELT having a better geographical resolution and a tendency of over-stating events compared to ICEWS (Ward et al., 2013). However, entity-relationship extraction is just one of the four steps required for narrative modeling. 32 

Topic Extraction. Topic extraction is a second step, although the sequence of the execution of the steps is irrelevant in this context. Same as with entity relationships, fast, inexpensive, automated topic extraction at a large enough scale was still a challenge when the narrative economics theory was formulated (Velden et al., 2017). Topic extraction endeavors to identify the topic of a narrative; in other words, pinpoint what the story is about as precisely and concisely as possible (Shiller, 2017). In essence, topic extraction identifies the meme, the thought virus the narrative transmits when shared. The more complex the story gets, the more difficult it becomes to narrow it down to a single topic, especially since many concurrent, equally valid perspectives can exist on any narrative (Velden et al., 2017). In the meantime, computer science solved this problem with the help of machine learning, neural networks, and artificial intelligence (Wadden et al., 2019) and optimized it by topic clustering methods (Abasi et al., 2021). Recognizing the co-existence and co-validity of a plethora of memes comprised in each narrative, Georgetown University's freely available GDELT dataset pre-coded 396 topics and themes based on the classification frameworks of Albaugh et al. (2013) and Leetaru and Schrodt (2013), interconnected within GDELT's Global Knowledge Graph (GKG). Nevertheless, entity-relationship and topic extraction are only half of the prerequisites of narrative modeling. The other half is comprised of subject modeling and emotion analysis. 

Subject Modeling. Emotions are not objective; they depend on the specific person, the human subject who feels them (Keltner et al., 2018). Subject modeling refers to creating a virtual persona with all the psychological attributes of the potential reader of a narrative. Subject modeling is reader-centric and strives to predict the reader's emotional reaction to the narrative (Shiller, 2017). Under this name, it is not common knowledge; but if explained in the form of: "it is what Cambridge Analytica did to allegedly tip the U.S.-presidential campaign in 2016," most people will suddenly know and simultaneously understand the 33 meaning of subject modeling. This time not computer science but private businesses have solved subject modeling with the help of psychology by applying the Big Five OCEAN personality model through algorithmic psychometrics (Stark, 2018). Dr. Kosinski has created personality profiles of the audience (Grassegger & Krogerus, 2016) by correlating patterns of public Facebook 'Like's with traditional NEO PI-R TM personality profiles from tens of thousands of research volunteers (Bachrach et al., 2012; Kosinski et al., 2013). Although the news of this created quite a bit of public outrage and triggered bipartisan legislation in the United States of America, like the Honest Ads Act (Barrett et al., 2021) requiring ads to be marked accordingly if they are personalized, the technology of subject modeling has nevertheless continued to evolve. Subject modeling is currently commercially available to any paying advertiser in the form of lookalike audiences on Facebook (Semerádová & Weinlich, 2019) or similar audiences on Google (Duvvuri, 2021). However, identifying the thought virus in the form of its topic or meme, extracting the entities with their relationships, and having a model of the reader subject is not sufficient for narrative modeling. 

Emotion Analysis. The last step of narrative analysis, namely emotion analysis, remains unsolved (Shiller, 2017; Shiller, 2020a). Mackintosh (2021) analyzed the current state of narrative analysis and calls for more research into the unsolved area of emotion analysis by using a multi-disciplinary approach to include other scientific disciplines, such as psychology and computer science. Emotion analysis is not to be confounded with sentiment analysis; a subtle distinction, especially for non-native English speakers. Sentiment analysis can be considered emotion analysis' little brother, posing a more straightforward, one-dimensional analysis problem. Sentiment analysis detects the positive or negative valence and high or low arousal level on a bipolar, linear, bidirectional spectrum (Sailunaz & Alhajj, 2019). Social media users are familiar with sentiment analysis and opinion mining tools such as smileys, emojis, and the thumbs-up/down feedback method below each social media 34 narrative. On the other hand, emotions are much more complex constructs located in non-linear multi-dimensional spaces, not necessarily directional or polar. Due to their complexity, emotions, as opposed to sentiment, could explain why a specific narrative is shared virally and, therefore, contain much more helpful information than sentiments (Xu et al., 2020). Emotions are not static; they change over time. Emotion analysis requires, therefore, a theoretical model to account for such dynamic change. 

Emotion Dynamics Theory 

The history of emotion dynamics theory starts with the work of Levenson and Gottman (1983), who studied emotions in marital interactions. Everyone's daily life experience confirms that emotions are not static. Levenson and Gottmann (1983) researched the rules by which emotions develop and change over time. An analogy can be made between Newton's law of motion (Ducheyne, 2017; Newton, 1687) and Levenson and Gottmann´s (1983) emotion dynamics theory. Newton´s laws enable mechanical movement simulations and predictions in a three-dimensional space (Ducheyne, 2017; Newton, 1687). Emotional dynamics allows for the same kind of simulations and predicts change in emotions over time (Becker et al., 2004). The temporal dimension of emotional dynamics can be conceived of as an interconnected emotional network, and the simulation of change employs the Bayesian statistical model that is at the basis of the functioning of the human brain (Krone et al., 2018). The most recent work and further development of emotion dynamics theory belongs to Kuppens and Verduyn (2017), defining the four principles of emotion dynamics theory: inertia, contingency, regulation, and interaction. A similarity to Newton's laws of motion can be identified not only in identically naming two of the four principles but also at the level of conceptualization. Newton's first law of inertia can be considered equivalent to the inertia principle in emotion dynamics theory. The principle of emotional contingency is the equivalent of Newton's second law describing the changes an external force can provoke in 35 the movement of a body if one substitutes the external force with an external event. The same is true for Newton's third law of action and reaction, which finds its equivalent in the emotion dynamics interaction principle. Only the principle of allostasis does not have a Newtonian equivalent because it requires desire, a fundamentally human characteristic without an equivalent in the movement of physical objects. Although gravity might have the same effects as desire when it comes to attraction, it is not helpful as a comparison because it only has a status quo while lacking the target status and intentionality of desire. Each of the four principles of emotion dynamics will be presented in-depth in the following paragraphs. 

Principle of Inertia. According to Kuppens and Verduyn (2017), the principle of inertia postulates that emotions are resistant to change and always tend to reflect the respective current emotional state. Similarly, according to Newton's first law of motion, physical bodies will continue to move or remain at rest unless acted upon by an external force (Ducheyne, 2017; Newton 1687). However, since it has been previously established that emotions are fundamentally dynamic, the comparison does not extend to the rest state of physical bodies but only to their dynamic state as emotions do not have a resting state equivalent. To extend the comparison for ease of understanding, Newton's first law of motion refers to an ideal motion and disregards friction. 

Similarly, the emotion dynamics principle of inertia disregards the waning over time of emotions, mainly because it is still unclear how long emotional arousal lasts, and the individual variance is too significant to allow for a generalization (Tambini et al., 2017). From a biological perspective, the principle of emotional inertia can be thought of as being the equivalent of the biological homeostasis of all living organisms. Homeostastis is the term coined by Cannon (1926) to delineate the name of the principle discovered by Bernard (1859). Homeostatis literally means standing still and describes the maintenance of a stable state. Self-loops are the most potent form of augmentation and temporal prolongation of an 36 existing feeling, especially for sadness and anxiety (Bringmann et al., 2016). For the purpose of this study, this principle of inertia can be operationalized straightforwardly by the assumption that if the topic of a narrative does not change, the principle of inertia will keep the emotion unchanged during the subsequent spread of the narrative should it go viral. Conversely, every mutation in the topic will trigger a change in emotion, as further described by the principle of contingency. 

Principle of Contingency. According to Kuppens and Verduyn (2017), the principle of contingency postulates that the change of an emotional state is typically triggered by external or internal events, often social, that raise concerns or influence the person's well-being, regardless of whether that influence is positive or negative. Analogously, in Newton's second law of motion, physical bodies will change their state of motion when a force acts upon them (Ducheyne, 2017; Newton, 1687). The similarity is evident if an emotional event substitutes the external physical force. However, neither the size of the change nor the intensity of the resulting emotion can be precisely measured or accurately calculated with a formula such as Newton conceived of. For the purpose of this study, this principle can be operationalized by the assumption that if the topic of a narrative mutates, the principle of contingency explains the change of emotion accordingly during the subsequent spread of the narrative, should it go viral. Bringmann et al. (2018) successfully tested the applicability of this principle with a semi-parametric time-varying vector-autoregressive (TV-VAR) model using the programming language and statistical software environment R. Nevertheless, since neither human emotions nor external factors or internal emotional states tend to be static over time, their dynamic changes cause interactions that can alter the effect the two principles described so far, have. 

Principle of Interaction. Newton's third law of motion, known as the law of action and reaction, describes mathematically how physical bodies behave when they interact and 37 trigger an exchange of forces acting upon each other (Ducheyne, 2017). According to Kuppens and Verduyn (2017), the principle of interaction postulates that all the other emotion dynamics principles interact similarly to Newton's third law of motion by boosting or canceling each other out dynamically. To date, there is no exact mathematical formula available like in physics to calculate the size of interaction or to quantify the interaction effect of emotions. Nevertheless, this principle can be operationalized by identifying separately but simultaneously the prerequisites of more than one of the emotion dynamics principles. The principle of interaction can explain a boosted or canceled effect that the application of either principle alone could not have explained but appears only as the result of their interaction. Yang and Shen (2021) successfully applied the principle of interaction using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Google's spatial-temporal-structured deep bidirectional transformer model for language understanding, called BERT (Devlin et al., 2018). Google´s BERT is a technological precursor of Microsoft´s ChatGPT (Wu et al., 2023). Uludag (2024) successfully applied emotion dynamics principles to ChatGPT 3.5 Turbo generated text. 

Since there are only three Newtonian laws of motion, this is how far the previously physics-based comparison goes. The last emotion dynamic principle does not apply to physical bodies but stems from biology being an exclusive expression and property of life itself. 

Principle of Regulation. The principle of regulation postulates that emotions tend to fit the desired emotional state to maintain allostasis. The term allostasis was coined by Sterling and Eyer (1988) to describe a biological adaptation of all living organisms to achieve stability through variability. Allostasis can be contrasted with homeostasis, which by extension of the analogy, would allow the principle of regulation to be opposable to the principle of inertia. The biological concept of allostasis was adapted in psychology within the concept of allostatic load by McEwen and Stellar (1993) and describes the maintenance of an 38 emotional arousal level triggered by stress, which is bell-shaped and exhibits at the peak the optimum stress level to maximize human performance. The theory of allostatic load allows for the operationalization of the principle of regulation without the necessity to include subject modeling to determine what the desired emotional state of the reader is by substituting it with the assumption that the peak of the bell curve of the allostatic load can be considered optimal (Guidi et al., 2021). The principle of regulation through a regression to the mean has been observed in the study of Naskar et al. (2020) in 63% of re-tweets on Twitter over time (based on an analysis of over 17 million tweets from almost 70.000 users mined between 2016 and 2017). For the purpose of this study, the principle of regulation would be expressed in a tendency of regression to the mean through time during the viral spread of a topic of all extreme emotions contingent with the topic from both the highly positive as well as the extreme negative end of the spectrum. As such, the principle of regulation can be conceptualized as an attenuator of the principle of emotional contingency as well as a specific and quantifiable expression of the principle of interaction. Krone et al. (2018) demonstrate in their longitudinal empirical research based on self-reported written material containing emotions from 50 volunteers that emotion dynamics theory is useful in emotion analysis. Using a vector autoregressive Bayesian model applied to text, the model was able to cope with missing values, and handle short, uni-, and multivariate time series of narratives such as this study analyzed (Krone et al., 2018). The 50 volunteers kept a diary describing their emotions and the topics that triggered them. The emotions and topics were extracted from these self-report, diary-type narratives using a vector autoregressive Bayesian model to create a time series of emotions. The correlation of the triggering topic with the emotion (principle of contingency) and the change of the emotions over time (principles of inertia and interaction) was found to be consistent with the predictions of emotion dynamics theory (Krone et al., 2018). Bringmann et al. (2018) used a 39 semi-parametric time-varying vector-autoregressive (TV-VAR) model to study operationalized emotion dynamics on empirical emotional text data from a dyadic cohabiting couple over the time period of three months and provided evidence for the usefulness of emotion dynamics theory in emotion analysis of narratives. It enabled dynamic emotion detection without a priori knowledge of the timing or nature of the upcoming emotional change. Bringmann et al.´s (2018) findings from their longitudinal study of empirical emotional data were consistent with the findings of Krone et al. (2018) from the analysis of the narratives contained in the diaries of 50 volunteers. In both studies a triggering topic (internal or external) was correlated with an emotion in the self-report narratives (principle of contingency) and the transposition of the emotions over time were both as predicted by emotion dynamics theory (principles of inertia and interaction). Berger et al. (2021) successfully operationalized emotion dynamics theory to analyze the user engagement over time of 30.000 online news articles; if user engagement over time were substituted with the re-distribution of online news articles, the present study could be considered a partial replication of the work of Berger et al. (2021). Emotion dynamics theory was operationalized by Berger et al. (2021) to quantify the volatility in the emotional content of written text and how it relates to engagement, whereas volatility was conceptualized as dynamic emotional change and engagement as a continued interest in following the topic of the narrative over time. Berger et al. (2021) concluded that the emotional dynamics or the volatility of the emotional content of a narrative was a significant mediator of the reader´s continued engagement with the narrative. Hipson and Mohammad (2021) applied emotion dynamics theory in an emotion analysis of the narratives contained in movie dialogues using the texts of the publicly available internet Movie Script Database (IMSDb) and found that the amount of time that a movie character was scripted to spend engaging with a narrative was significantly associated with its emotion density. These previous applications of emotion 40 dynamics theory in empirical emotion analysis research on narratives strengthen the case for its usage in the broader context of narrative economics. Choosing emotion dynamics theory for this study meant eliminating competing alternatives, which will be presented further on accompanied by the rationale for the deliberate choices that were made. 

Alternative Emotion Theories 

The criteria by which the theoretical frameworks have been chosen were utilitarian, in the sense that each theory should be able to explain either an economic or psycho-emotional aspect of how the emotions contained in narratives can influence social, political, health, or monetary factors. Alternative evolutionary, physiological, psychotherapeutic, philosophical, literary, artistic, and biological emotion theories will be shortly presented in the subsection dedicated to the literature review of emotions but were excluded due to their lack of operational usefulness to this study. A brief overview of excluded theories and the justification of exclusion will be presented below. Fear is used in an exemplary way as a primary emotion to test the applicability of the respective emotion theory to narrative analysis in the context of narrative economics. Fear has been chosen for exemplification and theory testing due to the human negativity bias; negative emotions are processed stronger and faster than positive ones (Norris, 2021). A plethora of different theories strive to explain emotions (Keltner et al., 2018). Schachter´s (1964) cognition-arousal theory of emotion conceptualizes emotions as a two-step process. A stimulus leads to physical arousal in the first step. In the case of fear, that stimulus is usually something threatening. Cognitive appraisal is the necessary second step to determine the exact nature of the emotion. When it comes to fear, the cognitive appraisal process assesses whether a stimulus qualifies as a fear-inducing threat in comparison to the coping mechanisms accessible to the individual. This theory combines a biological with a cognitive perspective, but the limitation of this theory is that cognition is not always a 41 necessary component of emotional affect. The cognitive-arousal theory has not been considered suitable to inform this study because neither the biological nor the cognitive perspective can be informative or operationalized in any helpful way to explore the role of emotions as mediators in narratives triggering economic consequences. The dimensional feeling model is a biological theory of emotion (Roy et al., 2012). According to this model, emotions have several bipolar dimensions: valence and arousal, and axes: positive/negative, approach/withdrawal. In the case of fear, for example, the axes approach or withdrawal corresponds to Walter Cannon's (1929) fight or flight catchphrase response (Bracha et al, 2004). The ventromedial prefrontal cortex is assumed to determine the affective meaning. On the plus side, this theory pinpoints the biological substrate of emotions, explains behavioral correlates, and aids emotion classification. The weakness of this model is that it cannot explain the socially constructed component of emotion. Fear of using public transport, fear of having no friends, or ihahamuka, the Rwandan genocide survivor´s fear of being unable to breathe (Otake & Tamming, 2021), for example, are socially constructed fears, which differ from one country to another (Burnham et al., 2016). The dimensional feeling model also has not been considered helpful because biological concepts are not informative in narrative analysis and due to the missing socio-cultural considerations. The network theory of emotion, a cognitive and neo-associationist model proposed by Berkowitz (1990), adds the socio-cultural aspects missing in the dimensional fear model. Berkowitz (1990; 2013) postulated that emotions are recorded as learned schemas, triggered upon recognition by the external stimuli with which they have been initially conditioned. In the case of fear, a notable experiment that reflects the schema of learned fright is Watson and Rayner's Little Albert, who was conditioned to be afraid of otherwise harmless fluffy rabbits (Crawford, 2015). While it explains the social construction of learned emotions through 42 schemas, the implication of this theory that every random stimulus could elicit any discretionary emotion seems rather implausible. Mizruchi (1994) criticized Berkowitz´s (1990) neo-associationist model because it disregards rational choice, the role of culture and norms, as well as human agency. The network theory of emotion has not been taken into consideration to inform this study because the neo-associationist concepts cannot be operationalized in narrative analysis and because of the lack of evidence for the postulate that random stimuli can be conditioned to cause discretionary emotions. The multitude of emotion classification systems and theories about the origin of emotions reflect the diversity and complexity of human emotions (Keltner et al., 2018). There are considerable overlaps between emotions and humans are often unsure of how to describe their complex feelings (Keltner et al., 2018). Russell´s (2003) cognitive core-affect theory takes this into account by assuming core affects as subunits, which come before emotions. Core affect has arousal levels and is situated on a continuum between pleasure and displeasure. It can have an internal or external cause, and core affect is not accessible through introspection. The process of emotion awareness assumes two stages: arousal followed by social construction. The core-affect theory is in this regard similar to Schachter´s (1964) cognition-arousal theory of emotion, but instead of postulating cognition as the second stage it substitutes it with a socially constructed element to account for cultural differences. In the case of fear, it assumes that instead of individuals deciding if something is worth fighting or fleeing from, society teaches what is worth engaging in and what should preferably be avoided. Russell´s theory provides a plausible explanation for overlapping feelings and the variability of emotions dependent on the particular social environment and the cultural history of the individual. However, it places little emphasis on neural substrates, fails to explain consciousness and has been excluded from this study because it entails no useful operationalization mechanism to the analysis of emotions contained in narratives. 43 There is considerable consensus in the scientific community on the theoretical possibility of identifying, naming, and counting basic emotions (Hutto et al., 2018). Defining a set of basic emotions would be useful in the context of emotion analysis in narratives because a clear classification makes automated, computer aided detection more likely. Here is a chronological selection of authors who have each empirically determined a set of basic, prototypical emotions: Shaver et al. (1987; 2001), Ekman (1992), Miller (1995), Martindale (1987; 2019), Plutchik (2001), Strapparava and Valitutti (2004), Neviarouskaya et al. (2007), Latinjak (2012), Ortony et al. (1988), Ortony and Turner (1990), Pennebaker et al. (2007), Robinson (2008), Steunebrink et al. (2009), Dodds et al. (2011), Loughran and McDonald (2011), or Cambria et al. (2012). The subsection discussing basic emotions contains a comparison of the sets of basic emotions each determined empirically. Although there is agreement that basic emotions per se exist (Hutto et al., 2018), due to contention on what exactly the set of basic emotions is, none of these empirical studies is useful as a single guiding theoretical framework. Since the one, all-encompassing theory of emotion has not been formulated or agreed upon by the scientific community, yet (Wang et al., 2020), utilitarian aspects were considered by this author the optimal selection criteria to identify and choose guiding theoretical frameworks. The criteria used were applicability to narratives with economic consequences and the possibility of operationalization for automated, computer aided emotion analysis in written text. By these utilitarian criteria, emotion dynamics and prospect theory were identified through an extensive literature research as being the most operationalizable emotion theories that can be applicable to emotion analysis in narratives in an automated, computer aided data exploration. Emotion dynamics theory was already presented, prospect theory follows next. 44 

Prospect Theory 

The psychologists Kahneman and Tversky (1979) developed the psycho-economic prospect theory because the paradigm of their contemporary homo economicus had entered the model crisis stage of the Kuhn-Cycle of scientific revolution (Kuhn, 1963). The homo economicus theory explained profit maximization as an entirely rational decision to buy goods at the lowest price and sell them at the highest price (Pareto & Page, 1906). The difficulty with this theory was that it entered the model crisis stage because the highest and lowest price could only be determined in hindsight and not during the unfolding of the market dictated price fluctuation (Sezer et al., 2017). Although technical indicators have been calculated for decades for this purpose using stock market technical analysis, not even the computer power available today has solved this issue of determining the perfect time to buy or to sell, as dictated by the homo economicus rationale (Dai et al., 2020) Prospect theory states that because people cannot make entirely rational economic decisions, they rely on more psychological factors like herd mentality and follow trends, tending to do what everybody else seems to be doing (Shantha, 2018). Kahneman and Tversky (1979) contrasted previous economic rationale by postulating that from a psychological perspective, people tend to buy when prices rise, motivated by fear of missing out (FOMO) and panic sell to cut their losses when prices fall, following the market trends through economic herd mentality. Barberis et al. (2016) successfully empirically tested the predictive power of prospect theory regarding economic decision-making related to the stock market. In the past, stocks with high performance triggered buying decisions in the U.S. stock market data from 1931 until 2010 and in the large majority of the 46 international markets from which the trading patterns were analyzed (Barberis et al., 2016). As a decision theory, prospect theory explains how a narrative is interpreted in deciding whether to buy or sell a particular publicly traded stock of a company mentioned in a viral story and can make, 45 through its reach, a global economic impact. Therefore, news stories have been routinely included to augment the traditional technical indicators in machine learning-based stock market trading bot models (Vargas et al., 2018). Ruggeri et al. (2020) replicated Kahneman and Tversky´s (1979) original study with 141 participants from 19 countries and found that 91% of all choices to buy or sell stock were motivated by trend as predicted by prospect theory and not by economic rationale. Shah et al. (2018) identified heuristic and choice biases as predicted by prospect theory in a sample of 143 investors trading on the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX). Chaudhry and Kulkarni (2021) analyzed the democratized investment trading apps Robinhood and Public and found the choice biases of prospect theory embedded in the design of the trading apps themselves. Ruggeri et al. (2020), Shah et al. (2018), and Chaudhry and Kulkarni (2021) all found evidence of herd behavior, of stock acquisitions and sales based purely on trending news and other trader’s actions used as a guideline, as prospect theory predicts, and not of the classical economic rationale of `sell high, buy low`. As such, a recent example of applied narrative economics and prospect theory were the GameStop and AMC Theatres stock hypes via Reddit (Chaudhry & Kulkarni, 2021). AMC Theatres and GameStop stocks are meme stocks. Meme stocks is the term coined for a sort of trading based on a narrative and driven by the type of herd mentality explained by prospect theory (Aloosh et al., 2021; Costola et al., 2021). In an effort to educate small investors on how to overcome the choice biases predicted by prospect theory, idle games such as Robinhood´s Forest have been designed to discourage impulse investment based on news feeds (Chaudhry & Kulkarni, 2022). Pelster (2017) identified the applied elements of both narrative economics and prospect theory in the trading behavior of small investors of the social trading platform eToro. Pelster (2017) found that increased audience spread was a predictor of influence, consistent with the tenets of narrative 46 economics and that past returns of an investor on eToro were used as a basis of judging future success, as predicted by prospect theory. 

Prospect Theory in Collective/Macro Level Decision Making 

Prospect theory is a theory developed originally with the purpose of explaining individual decisions (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Most the amounts of economic consequences expressed in USD, EUR, and GBP analyzed in this dissertation referring to the topics in Table 9 are political and macro-economic topics, reflecting collective /macro level behavior. A legitimate question might rise, if prospect theory is applicable to collective behavior. Although collective decision making is outside of the scope of the original theory, meta-analysis have validated an increasing amount of evidence suggesting that prospect theory does apply for political decision making as well (Vis, 2011). The basis for extending this individual micro level decision making theory within the political realm and to public policy is the fact that prospect theory is based on four neurological cognitive biases: the certainty effect, loss aversion, the status quo bias, and the negativity effect that apply on an aggregated level in the same way as they apply individually (Bellé et al., 2018). Especially loss aversion is a well documented effect of aggregated decision making in the political sciences (Alesina, & Passarelli, 2019), which mirrors the loss aversion in individual decision making as stated in prospect theory verbatim "losses loom larger than gains" (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979, p. 279). Loss aversion is aggravated by the status quo bias; the individual tendency to resist change because its disadvantages are more prominent and present than its advantages (Kahneman et al., 2000), for which strong cross-disciplinary evidence exists of also at a collective and aggregated political and macro-economic decision-making level (Godefroid et al., 2023). In democracies, the route via which individual decision-making influences political decision making is through voting, to which all the biases of prospect theory apply (Passarelli & Del Ponte, 2020). In between election cycles, it is the role of the 47 press as the fourth estate to hold governments apprised on public sentiment and opinion (Soroka & McAdams, 2015). The media´s impact on political decision making and policy is created by influencing governamental risk perception via media frames (Touri, 2006). The risk of not being re-elected is perceived higher by a government if the decisions and policies go against the public sentiment as expressed by the press and media outlets, while the chance of reward (re-election) is perceived higher if policies are alligned with the media frames of the narratives from news cycle (Ahva & Steensen, 2019). To take into account and include narratives in an economic theory has only recently been considered (Shiller, 2017). The bulk of the previous research into narratives comes from other scientific disciplines, such as psychology, social sciences, anthropology, education, journalism, marketing, and the humanities, and will be discussed in-depth in the literature review section dedicated in turn to narratives, emotions, and applied emotion analysis in narratives. 

Literature Review of Narratives 

Storytelling is the basis of human understanding and socialization, of how we see and interpret the world (McAdams, 2019). The origins of storytelling go back to the depths of human history. While it is impossible to know for sure who told the first story, the paintings on the walls of the caves in Lascaux, France, are estimated to be over 20,000 years old and are considered to be one of the oldest painted European narratives discovered so far (Ducasse & Langlais, 2019). The functions and forms of narratives have undergone the same transformation as societies did, from the primitive communities that told stories through their oral history myths and artistic ornaments, right up to the digital narratives of today (Yılmaz & Ci ğerci, 2019). Narratives have discernable structure elements, such as the plot (overcoming the monster, rags to riches, voyage, return, comedy, tragedy, rebirth), characters (hero, villain, maiden, king), are emotionally engaging, have take-away lessons or a call-to-48 action (Boyd et al., 2020). The exact number and classification system of types of stories is still debated; Propp (1984) distinguished 31 functional types of narratives, Tobias (1999) found 20 master plots, while Booker (2004) reduced the entire literature to only seven basic plots. Klages (2006) considered any such reductive classification efforts as dehumanizing altogether, while Morson and Schapiro (2017) called for an increase in the same to enable an improvement in economic modeling. Before the invention of writing, dance and music, together with the rhymes of poetry, are now acknowledged as the ancestral predecessors of storytelling, of proper narratives as we know them today (Terry, 2018). This was not always the case. Up until the 19th century, when European explorers encountered pre-literate tribes, the meaning their dances carried was not recognized as narratives (Pound, 1919). The Christian Church did not initially recognize these "primitives" as humans due to a lack of recognizable socialization stories that were understandable to the European Christian explorers (Yılmaz & Ci ğerci, 2019). The myths that narratives of pre-literate cultures conveyed were the earliest forms of history, religion, and science, incipient theogony, cosmogony, anthropogony, and eschatology all in one (Yılmaz & Ci ğerci, 2019). With the invention of writing, narratives were gradually given a more structured form culminating with the organized scheme of the academic methods of today that narratives have in many scientific disciplines such as psychology, law, theology, computer science (artificial intelligence), literary theory, journalism, marketing, or economics (Yılmaz & Ci ğerci, 2019). Each of these sciences studies the concept of narratives under its own specific name. The multitude of synonyms for narratives makes a comprehensive and exhaustive literature review difficult, mainly because each scientific discipline uses a different name for its domain-specific exploration of narratives (Shaffer et al., 2018). In marketing, narratives are referred to as testimonials (Kilian, 2018; Rahman, 2019). In journalism, narratives are researched under the keyword of exemplars and used on purpose as pars per toto carriers 49 (Oschatz et al., 2021; Skovsgaard & Hopmann, 2020; Zerback & Peter, 2018). In psychology, narratives can be found primarily in qualitative research case histories or case studies (Lawless & Chen, 2019). Oral history investigates narratives as sagas or myths (Jackson, 2019; Passerini, 2021). Sociology is interested in narratives as personal stories to transmit a cultural norm (Polletta & Redman, 2020). The diversity of viewpoints and research interests makes a universally valid definition of narratives difficult and hinders interdisciplinary consensus upon their classification and characterization (Shaffer et al., 2018). Narratives are such a unique and integral part of what makes us human that some scientists have proposed to change the Latin term homo sapiens of our species. Fisher (1994) proposed the name homo narrans, Gould (1994) suggested homo narrator, and Ferrand and Weil (2001) put forward homo narrativus instead of homo sapiens. The multitute of scientific disciplines, each contributing an essential and integral part of a holistic understanding of narratives, have yet to reach consilience. As such, no single scientific discipline can provide a comprehensive, integrative model of how narratives work, the effect they have, their components, or their classification. Only the educational, shaping effect of narratives is consensus-capable across these diverse scientific disciplines (Shaffer et al., 2018). For most children, stories are the first step of socialization, the first contact with the culture they were born into (Wahman et al., 2022). Nativists and empiricists agree that stories are what implicitly teach children their native language in context, help them acquire the correct grammar effortlessly, and are second in immersive exposure frequency only to lullabies (Mirski & Gut, 2020). The anecdotal evidence from the few documented cases of feral children shows that in the absence of stories in the critical years of language acquisition, one can never learn to speak and that stories make us human in behavior (Roux, 2021). The immersiveness, frequency, and universality of exposure of children to stories from birth thus make it understandable why narratives are known by many names to many people (stories, 50 legends, myths, sagas, tales, fables), both in simple lay terms as well as in scientific research (Gabriel, 2018). Due to this early and constant exposure to narratives, education has taken a particular interest in them and produced different theories to explain their effect on children's development. Jean Piaget (1928; 2009) is known to be the father of constructivism, an epistemological theory of learning positing that children construct their reality rather than receive knowledge through direct transmission. Further developing this idea in his constructionist theory, Papert (1980) identified narratives as the tools children use to learn about the world and construct their understanding of reality. Kegan (1982) went so far as to assume that narratives, besides being the tools to build an interpretation of the world around us, also develop the self-image, the qualia of understanding one's self. Not only are narratives in the form of children's stories the primary tools for socialization in any culture, but they also construct the moral imperative, the distinction of what is considered right or wrong in a specific society (Bénabou et al., 2018). Narratives are the stories we share to help make sense of our common human experience; they help explain, organize, predict, and justify; they are the instruments the mind uses to construct reality itself (Bruner, 1991a; Bruner, 1991b). The story of our own life is also constructed and remembered as an affective, personal, sensemaking narrative continuously shaped, re-shaped, changed, and reconstructed by repeated narration during a person's lifetime (Alea, 2018; Adler, 2019). Besides personal reality construction, narratives also make sense of other people's realities; they help give meaning to facts, events, and cope with randomness through the collective sensemaking of a shared narrative (Bietti et al., 2019). The advent of social media turned collective sensemaking into an echo chamber created by the filter bubble of associating exclusively with a self-enforcing, like-minded social in-group (Dutti et al., 2017). Not only can narratives help make sense of the world, but they can also be a source of 51 justification for action (Shiller, 2017). Especially within prospect theory and narrative economics frameworks, the narrative's function of action justification is the most prevalent (Bénabou et al., 2018). Working under these epistemological assumptions of a constructed reality and interpreting narratives as the construction tools of the mind containing in the form of parables the moral compass of what is right and wrong to justify action, the assumption that narratives can be used to create economic momentum becomes almost a logical conclusion (Bénabou et al., 2020; Juille & Jullien, 2016). A narrative does not have to be true or factually accurate to serve as a call to action or potentially alter a person's belief system (Bénabou et al., 2020; Shiller, 2020a). The pars pro toto fallacy, the confounding of correlation with causation, base-rate neglect, as well as motivated reasoning are some of the statistical causes why simple, emotion-laden argument cues are successful action triggers for viral transmission of a narrative (Gailiu šyt ė, 2022; Kahan, 2013), regardless of its factfulness (intended meaning Rosling, 2019). Vosoughi et al. (2018) found in their analysis of a 2006-2017 dataset from Twitter that false news reached an up to 100 times bigger audience through re-tweeting than truth. Exemplars, the name by which narratives in the news are researched in journalism, are of particular interest in this regard because, in a post-factum era, the statistical fallacies mentioned above can be used on purpose to trigger viral sharing on social media (Peter, 2019). The next section provides an in-depth review of the role of exemplars in virality and the emotions they carry. 

Exemplars - Narratives in the News 

Declining interest in printed newspapers, traditionally financed via subscriptions and advertising, forced a shift in journalism to an audience-based financing model (Olsen et al. 2021). In the age of the internet, journalists' primary Key Performance Indicator (KPI) is how much interest their articles present to the readers, measured by the traffic they attract, mainly, 52 the number of clicks their stories have generated (Lischka & Garz, 2021). The clicks from the readers are converted into income for the news outlet through online advertising, incentivizing each journalist to generate interest by whatever means necessary, which leads to the rather frown upon practice of clickbaiting, thereby reducing the journalistic quality and credibility (Molyneux & Coddington, 2020). As part of the research project titled “Politainment in the post-truth environment: new narratives, clickbait and gamification” (reference CSO2017-84472-R), funded by the National Plan for Research, Development and Innovation of the Ministry of Economy and Competitiveness of Spain, Bazaco et al. (2019) found that the proportion of clickbait style titles in newspapers was 41.6%. Kaushal and Vemuri, K. (2021) discovered that in the United States the percentage of clickbait type titles of traditional media outlets increased from 24.12% when printed to almost half of the narratives (47.56%) when shared on broadcast media, while non-mainstream, presumably less reliable media used clickbait titles in 45.82% of their content. Although the information content of the narrative remains the same, changing the distribution channel from print to broadcast media doubled the use frequency of the clickbait strategy, even in reputable news oriented broadcast media outlets such as CNN or NBC (Rony et al., 2017). In an effort to regain the trust of the readers without reducing the clickbaiting effect, journalists are striving to put a human face to their reporting by using personal stories of ordinary people or by harvesting the crowd-pulling effect of celebrities' and influencers' illustrative individual stories (Wheatley, 2020). Machill et al. (2007) empirically determined in their reception analysis with 215 participants that fact reporting in the news is retained and comprehended significantly less by the control group audience than an exemplar narrative with a relatable protagonist by the experimental group audience. Romney and Johnson (2020) partially replicated Machill et al.´s (2007) research with 2,000 images on Instagram and found 53 comparable results; the images representing narrative messages received significantly more engagement. Exemplars are, in journalism, the academic equivalent of private stories shared by friends about somebody they know personally, which leads to an integral judgment of the described phenomenon, although only a single instance or part of it is known. Their Bayesian pars pro toto effect has been studied by exemplification theory (Lachlan, 2020; Zillmann, 1999). Exemplification theory employs mathematical concepts such as base rate together with heuristics borrowed from the computer and information science, especially useful in database optimization, such as encoding, storage, processing, and retrieval, combined with psychological concepts of emotional arousal (Bigsby et al., 2019). The mechanism of the role of emotions in the effect of exemplars is challenging to study in a laboratory setting, leading to contradicting results unless the subject-modeling of the reader is taken into account (Klemm et al., 2019). The psychological phenomenon mediating the persuasive effect of exemplars is explored under the topic of narrative persuasion (Oschatz et al., 2021). The strength of the narrative's persuasion depends on the similarity of the reader with the character presented in the exemplar (Ooms et al., 2019). Because it is such a central concept, it is worth diving deeper into understanding the pars pro toto cognitive process underlying exemplars' workings. One theory about consciousness is that the brain interprets sensory input as semiotic; it translates the signs within the perception of the environment into consciousness (Petrilli & Ponzio, 2018). At the first encounter, each instance is interpreted as a whole, a synecdoche, stereotypically representative of the entire category under Bayesian logic. During all subsequent encounters, the stereotypical category model is updated (Glasauer, 2019). For instance, if a child's initial encounter with a swan involved seeing a white one, this early experience would establish the stereotype that all swans are white. The stereotype would strengthen with every subsequent 54 white swan until and unless the first black swan encountered challenges the implicit color assumption. However, the categories the brain creates from the information it processes can be situationally flexible (Petrilli & Ponzio, 2018). A white swan can represent the category of white swans, swans, birds, or even all animals, depending on the specific circumstances. The persuasive power of a narrative also depends on the frequency of the encounter of that specific category. The first encounter always has the highest impact because it initializes the stereotype with 100% and becomes representative of the whole category via the pars pro toto Bayesian brain mechanism (Glasauer, 2019). Initializing the stereotype with 100% means that the first instance is generalized and provides the prototype for all further instances; if the first swan encountered is white, all other swans are expected to be white as well (McElreath, 2020). The narrative persuasion effect is amplified if the reader considers themselves contained in the category of the character depicted in the exemplar an inclusion extending the newly formed pars pro toto category to the reader, making them feel personally affected (Feng et al., 2021). An inclusive category can be as broad as gender, skin color, nationality, or something more personal like a shared illness, school, or employer (Jaber-Lopez et al., 2021). Exemplars can trigger, via the afore-described process, the subjective feeling that the character's story could also happen to the reader personally (Ooms et al., 2019). However, identification with the character's category from the exemplar alone is insufficient to trigger an action from the reader; the emotions embedded in the exemplar are the decisive arousal activating factor (Heiselberg & Skovsgaard, 2021). News reports in general also initialize a perceptual readiness and set the subjective probability level of an event (Siddle & Spinks, 2021), a phenomenon also known as Tuchman´s law (Tuchman, 1978). The effects exemplars have, determine their relevance, which is why the effect will be discussed in more detail in the next paragraph. 55 

Social, Political, Health, and Economic Effects of Narratives 

'If it happened to XYZ, then it could happen to me/us' - also known as self-referencing, is the main persuasive effect of narratives in the media (Weiss, 2022). One of the most contagious narratives with social, political, health, and economic effects presented in the media and shared through social media during the timespan 2019-2022 was the Covid-19 narrative, which spread with comparable speed as the virus (Shiller, 2020a). Powerful pandemic narratives tend to spread in constellations and produce confluences (Shiller, 2020a). One of the co-epidemics of the Covid-19 narrative was the anti-vaxxer movement (Ortiz- Sánchez et al., 2020). The anti-vaxxer movement first emerged in the 18th century as a reaction to the first vaccine against smallpox presented in 1796 by Jenner to the Royal Society of London, which prompted in 1867 the formation of the League against Mandatory Vaccination of London (Ortiz- Sánchez et al., 2020). Vaccine hesitancy gained momentum in 1998 when Andrew Wakefield published on a case series of only 12 children in The Lancet 

linking autism in children to MMR vaccines (Wakefield, 1998; 1999). MMR vaccination rate in the UK dropped by 9% in the year after the publication of Wakefield´s study (Segura Benedicto, 2012; Ortiz- Sánchez et al., 2020). Although his research was proven to be false, retracted by The Lancet (The Editors of The Lancet, 2010), and the UK General Medical Council's Fitness to Practise Panel revoked Wakefield´s medical license over it in 2010, the parental concerns over vaccinating their children remained and led to a global increase in the anti-vaccine movement (Balestra, 2016; Dean, 2021; Goldenberg, 2021). At the beginning of the 21th century, it produced hesitance only against the childhood vaccines, but during the global COVID-19 pandemic, it became a worldwide concern through an increasing refusal rate of vaccination against the SARS-CoV-2 virus (Dean, 2021). Through self-referencing and similar to the parental concerns of potentially causing autism in their babies as a side effect of MMR vaccines, each exemplar report in the news of 56 singular cases of side effects of the COVID-19 vaccine increased vaccine hesitancy and refusal rates (Benoit & Maldin, 2021). The effect of case reporting in the media was further amplified by the lack of transparency about the potential side effects of vaccines (Bearth & Siegrist, 2022). Montano (2022) analyzed the self-reports of side effects from the US vaccine adverse event reporting system (VAERS) and the EU self-report platform EudraVigilance and compared them with the 30-40 side effects contained in the Federal Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA) product information sheets of the COVID-19 vaccines approved for emergency use. Montano (2022) found 941 side effects on EudraVigilance and 816 on VAERS that were considered severe for seven of the major common toxicity criteria (CTC) drug toxicity categories and with sufficient signal strength to be significant. Montano (2020), in their analysis of the self-reports on the VAERS and EudraVigilance platforms, found severe adverse reactions like hemorrhage, pulmonary, neurological, gastrointestinal, thrombosis, and sexual organ reactions for seven major CTC drug toxicity categories. These severe side effects were not contained in the FDA and EMA-approved product information sheets of the COVID-19 vaccines (Montano, 2020). Exemplars headlines with COVID-19 vaccine side effects are effective clickbait, fueling vaccine hesitance through self-referecing with significant health, social, and economic consequences (Ahmad Kamboh et al., 2022). No Ice to Break: Rediscovering Our Community

Leading Americ an and Chinese scholars were quite uncomfortable when they arrived at the opening session
of a conference in early July 2023 on the c ampus of Peking Universit y. For most, this was the very first time
they had been in a meeting face to face with scholars from the other country in over three and a half years.
The intervening period had seen the unleashing of a global pandemic that took millions of lives and c aused
immense suffering and hardship. Moreover, the official U.S.-China relationship had deteriorated dramatic ally,
leading to esc alating tensions, tough talk, and sanc tions. But what was more important than the pandemic
or geopolitics that morning was the temperature, which hovered around 100 °F (~38 °C) and left everyone
dripping in sweat, making them even more anxious.

But once inside, with the aid of air conditioning and friends, temperatures quickly cooled and the
spirits of those present lifted. Within about five minutes, you could hear a collective sigh of relief as the
conversation picked up pace, with experts from both countries putting forth a range of views on issues
large and small. Consensus? No. All issues immediately out on the table? No. But a willingness to be
candid in a spirit of collegialit y? Absolutely. As one of the Chinese scholars recalled, “We opened up with
a sense of camaraderie right away.” There was no ice to break, not only because of the high temperatures,
but because American and Chinese scholars have deep ties that a pandemic and political frictions could
not easily extinguish.

That said, the resumption of U.S.-China scholarly ties was far from guaranteed, and the obstacles to their full
and healthy blossoming still exist. The original hope and the remaining challenges are the reason for this
initiative and this volume.

Origins

Scholarly exchange has been an important feature of U.S.-China relations since at least the 1850s. When the
United States and the People’s Republic of China (PRC) established diplomatic relations in 1979, the very first
agreement President Jimmy Carter and Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping signed was the “U.S.-China Science and
Technology Cooperation Agreement,” which created a foundation for scholarly ties. In the subsequent four
dec ades, the relationship expanded dramatic ally. Millions of Chinese and tens of thousands of Americ ans
have studied in undergraduate and graduate programs in the other country. Chinese universities substantially
revised their struc ture and curriculum across disciplines, often drawing inspiration from the United States
and other advanced industrialized countries. Professors and think tank scholars from both sides have c arried
out extensive field work on their own and in collaboration with their counterparts in the other country. This
includes not just foreign polic y experts from the other side, but scholars across all disciplines, including
science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), the social sciences, and humanities. Universities
and research organizations have also established thousands of institutional relationships supporting the
ac tivities of students, scholars, and each side’s broader societies.

About This Initiative

It is in this complex climate that the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and Peking Universit y
have attempted to provide leadership in the rebuilding of bilateral scholarly ties in order to avoid a more
permanent scholarly decoupling. In 2022, in the midst of the pandemic, Wang Jisi, the founding president of
Peking Universit y ’s Institute of International and Strategic Studies (IISS), and Scott Kennedy of CSIS engaged
in a pair of individual exchanges meant to break the ice.2 They both held meetings over several weeks with the
scholarly and polic y communities in each other’s countries.

On the foundation of that initial exchange, CSIS and Peking Universit y mutually agreed to scale up
their efforts and facilitate the exchange of leading experts from both countries across a wide range of
disciplines. In July 2023, a delegation of 12 U.S. scholars visited Beijing and held a closed-door conference
with 17 Chinese scholars hosted by IISS in the North Pavilion on the campus of Peking Universit y. Under
the conference title “Rebuilding China-U.S. Scholarly Exchange,” the participants exchanged views on
recent developments in universities and think tanks in both countries, the opportunities and challenges
of field research, and the prospects of U.S.-China scholarly collaboration, including among students,
scholars, and institutions. In October 2023, the scholars from both countries (12 from Chinese institutions
and 18 from U.S. ones) held the second of the initiative’s t wo conferences at CSIS’s headquarters
in Washington, D.C. Titled, “U.S.-China Scholarly Cooperation in an Era of Greater Geo-Strategic
Tensions,” the participants discussed the value of scholarly collaboration, the challenges to exchanges
posed by domestic social and political trends, strategies for navigating and managing national securit y
concerns, and potential principles for managing scholarly ties. In both Beijing and Washington, scholars
supplemented the conferences with additional private meetings with government officials, business
executives, journalists, and other scholars.

The pair of conferences witnessed a great deal of intensive brainstorming. Although there were
substantial disagreements, participants were open-minded, and the discussion throughout included a
minimum of superficial comments considered to be politically correct. That was in part made clear by the
fact that there were as many differences of opinion within both the U.S. and Chinese sides as there was
bet ween them.

About This Volume

The U.S. and Chinese participants to the conferences in Beijing and Washing ton were invited to contribute
essays on the topics raised during the meetings. Those essays compose the current volume. Scholars had
wide latitude in selec ting issues to address, and the projec t team encouraged everyone to express their own
perspec tives to facilitate a vigorous debate and did not attempt to reach a collec tive common point of view.
This volume adheres to this goal.

The contributions in Sec tion I consider the reasons why scholarly collaboration bet ween the United States
and China is valuable. Authors evaluate the costs and benefits to the ac ademic enterprise itself and to the t wo
societies. Several grapple with the debate about the national securit y implic ations of extensive scholarly ties.

The essays in Sec tion II examine the components of scholarly exchange and collaboration, including
institutions (such as universit y departments), the Fulbright Program, research data, and public ations. Each
author identifies current problems and proposes specific solutions.

In Sec tion III, the discussion shifts to consider the issue of scholarly exchange and collaboration through the lens of
several disciplines. Authors weigh in on issues facing international relations and securit y studies, climate change,
area studies, economics, history, and artificial intelligence. This sec tion exhibits the widest range of views about
the opportunities and risks in different fields and sug gestions about how best to move forward. A straightforward
interpretation of the contributions sug gests that progress has varied across fields, a pattern that may continue.
However, there is an opportunit y for more uniform progress if best prac tices are shared across disciplines.

The final contribution to the volume attempts to brings the various strands of the analysis together. Although
unconditional and fully open scholarly ties bet ween the t wo countries are unlikely for the foreseeable
future, outright scholarly decoupling is also improbable, in part bec ause it would be highly detrimental and
unnecessary. The essay considers proposals for how to most effec tively c alibrate the extent of scholarly ties to
maximize their benefits to the t wo societies while also minimizing the attendant risks.
